title: The Educated Barbarian: Hagakure analysis (part. 11)
summary: NH continues his Hagakure reading, focusing on passages about the path having no end, single-minded pursuit of one way, the weight of words, resolve, holding your own standards, and talent needing decades to mature. He links each passage to lifting, especially to rejecting the natural limit.
claims: Training is its own pursuit: the exertion itself is the goal, even when it doesn't produce the results you want
The best way to keep training forever is to enjoy the process; without enjoyment you'll quit at the first obstacle
A training that has an end has no point; like a game capped at level 100, people quit once there's nothing left to improve
Believing in the natural limit is a self-fulfilling prophecy: you stop pushing, your body stops evolving, and you meet the 'end' you imagined
Even if training isn't your top priority, making it a fixed part of your schedule keeps it pure; training only when you feel like it doesn't have the same impact
Pursuing two physical ways at once, like boxing and bodybuilding, pulls you in opposite directions and prevents excelling at either
Other pursuits are fine if they serve your main way: read science only insofar as it improves your training; if it takes away from training it's a hindrance
Verbal commitments increase follow-through; studies show people who commit out loud are more likely to act
What you repeat to yourself becomes your identity: acting timid in small things primes you to be timid when it matters
The point of 'nothing is impossible' is to remove the limits in your mind; if real limits exist nature will remind you
New Year's resolutions fail because people aren't truly resolved; if you can't promise yourself you'll do it, it's over
Adapting your standards to whoever you're with leads to a slow loss of identity; don't stoop to rude people's level
Spend your energy fully until 40; it won't magically reappear at 60, so be strong-headed in your 20s and 30s
Moralisers often don't follow their own doctrine; truly righteous people lead by example rather than proselytising
Men in their 30s who avoid responsibility and chase pleasure will regret it; humans are already wired for immediate gratification, so adopt a philosophy that opposes it
Talent is double-edged: gifted people start higher and climb faster, then become conceited when they reach levels without peers; real mastery takes 20-30 years
